To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

obese, slow-growing, feral pigs had a lower in vitro lipolytic rate per 100 mg fat mass than did fast-growing, lean pigs at the same age and weight; however, the obese pigs had a greater lipolyc response per total fat mass than did lean pigs.
at equal weight, the fast-growing, lean pig had less body fat and greater protein content than the slow-growing, obese pig.

the obese pig is characterized by a greater percent body and subcutaneous fat at equal age and equal weight, a lower in vivo lipolytic response to DBcAMP, and an increased number of nuclei per gram muscle at equal age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of genetic selection for growth rate on body composition, lipid metabolism and skeletal musculature in swine.
the effects of growth rate and body composition on lipid metabolism and muscle characteristics in pigs.
the relationship between body composition and in vitro adipose and muscle metabolism in fast- and slow-growing pigs of equal age and weight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
obese pigs are not necessarily less efficient in converting feed into lean tissue.
the obese, slow growing pig is a model for the obese human in that it has a greater percent bodyfat and backfat thickness, but at equal weight, a lower percent body protein.
the obese pig has an increased capacity for fat deposition and a reduced capacity for muscle deposition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the obese pigs were not only more obese but also had a lower capacity for lipid metabolism and muscle growth than lean, fast-growing pigs at equal weight and at equal age.

the slow growing, obese pigs were able to deposit more fat and less muscle than the fast-growing, lean pigs at equal body weight and that the differences in body composition were not due to differences in lipid metabolism.
the slow-growing obese pig has a greater capacity for lipid deposition than the fast-growing, lean pig.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the obese pig, Ossabaw, has a greater capacity for lipolysis than the lean pig.
the obese pigs were not as obese at the same weight as the lean pigs were at the same age.
the obese pigs were more efficient than the lean pigs in converting feed to body weight gain, but this advantage was lost as the pigs aged.
